newsitem.title: USA: Dlr begins higher in US, EMU concerns bruise mark.
newsitem.headline: Dlr begins higher in US, EMU concerns bruise mark.

text.p: The dollar started the week sharply higher against the mark after a win by the left in French general elections on Sunday heightened uncertainty about Europe's plans for a single currency, dealers said.
The combined left won 318 seats in the 577-member National Assembly. French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin will take over from conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Tuesday.
"There seems to be...safe haven buying in the dollar and also a little bit in sterling against the rest of Europe," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.

Strauss cited concern that monetary union will be delayed as well as "fear of what the Socialist are going to do, despite the fact that they say they are committed to honoring all of France's previous agreements."
The Socialist favor a less stringent interpretation of the criteria that has to be met to qualify for the proposed single European currency, which is slated to debut in January 1999.
The dollar opened at 1.7265/75 marks, up from 1.7050/60 marks at Friday's close. Against the yen, the dollar rose to 116.62/67 from 116.20/30.
Sterling also gained against the German unit, trading near 2.8165/75 marks shortly after the opening compared with around 2.8158/68 in early dealings.
Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland, said there is a "very good chance" the dollar will break above 1.73 marks on Monday.
Jury noted that 1.7370 marks was a point of "significant resistance" in April. "So, that's our immediate target."
"I think the people are realizing that the safe thing to buy in this scenario is the dollar," he said.

On Monday, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said he would try to reach an agreement with the Bundesbank before proposing legal changes that would allow Bonn to benefit from a revaluation of the Bundesbank's gold and foreign exchange reserves.
However, Waigel also said he would proceed with the effort to change the law without the Bundesbank's assent.
The revaluation would free up cash that could be used to reduce Germany's budget deficit and help it qualify for the single European currency.

Foreign Exchange Analytics partner David Gilmore said the German government's determination to press ahead with the revaluation plan and the fact that the new French goverment is likely to seek a loosening of the Maastricht criteria point to a weaker Euro.

Turning from developments in Europe, the dollar shrugged off news that U.S. personal income and consumption both rose a modest 0.1 percent in April. Economists polled by Reuters, on average, had expected personal income and consumption to be unchanged in April.

Also set for release on Monday is the National Association of Purchasing Management's report on business at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. The index is expected to slip to 53.9 in May from 54.2 in the previous month, based on the Reuter poll.
Elsewhere, the dollar opened at 1.4350/60 Swiss francs, up from 1.4140/50 francs at the previous close.
Sterling fell to $1.6315/25 from $1.6405/15.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3762/67 from C$1.3770/80.
The Australian dollar opened at $0.7600/05 compared with $0.7598/03.
